title: Are Scale-Free Networks Rare? Barabási–Albert Preferential Attachment, Vanishing Epidemic Thresholds & Hub Fragility vs. Clauset–Broido's 928-Network Audit & Lognormal Realism — From Barabási's metabolic hubs, Pastor-Satorras & Vespignani's vanishing epidemic threshold (lambda_c = <k>/<k^2> -> 0), and Albert, Jeong & Barabási's Achilles'-heel hub attack theorem through Holme & Kim's clustering critique, Clauset–Shalizi–Newman's takedown of log-log OLS (R^2 = 0.9788 on a pure lognormal!), and Broido & Clauset's 928-network audit finding only 4% Strongest scale-free support

teenKit.tldr: For decades, scientists thought everything from the internet to brain cells followed a single universal "scale-free" math law, but a massive 928-network audit proved that rule is actually super rare.
teenKit.whyItMatters: Understanding whether complex systems have fragile hubs or act like predictable grids changes how we stop global pandemics, prevent power grid blackouts, and protect the internet from cyber attacks.
keyTakeaways: Spatial networks like city streets are democratic and evenly spread, while unconstrained networks like airport maps create massive, dominating mega-hubs.
The famous Barabási-Albert model claimed networks grow scale-free through "preferential attachment," where rich nodes get richer by collecting more connections.
Modern statistical audits revealed that old methods faked power-law graphs using lazy log-log plots, and true scale-free networks only show up about 4% of the time.

vocab.meaning: A network whose connection distribution follows a power law, meaning a few nodes have massive numbers of links while most have very few.
The mathematical rule where new nodes joining a network prefer to connect to nodes that already have a lot of connections.
A statistical shortcut using straight lines on a log-scale graph that tricked researchers into seeing power laws where none actually existed.
A rigorous statistical referee used to objectively prove whether real-world data fits a true power law or a standard lognormal curve.

quiz.question: Why can't a physical city street grid look like an airline flight map?
options: Airports are managed by private companies
Roads are physically constrained by geography and space
Cities change sizes faster than computer networks
quiz.explanation: Streets are bound by physical space and geometry, making it impossible to cram 10,000 roads into a single intersection.

quiz.question: What did Anna Broido and Aaron Clauset's audit of 928 networks reveal about scale-free networks?
options: They govern every known biological system
They are completely imaginary and never exist
They are actually quite rare, with only 4% showing strong support
They only appear in computer routers
quiz.explanation: Their massive 2019 audit found that true power-law behavior is rare, with lognormal distributions dominating real data.

quiz.question: How did early scientists accidentally fake scale-free network results for twenty years?
options: By drawing straight lines on log-log plots without proper statistical testing
By using too many computers in their simulations
By studying human friendships instead of the internet
quiz.explanation: Simple log-log Ordinary Least Squares regression made curved data look like a straight power-law line, fooling researchers into false confidence.
